title: init, add, commit, log
summary: Start a repository, build commits one snapshot at a time, and read history with git log.

steps.title: Your first repository
body: git init                     # create .git/ in the current folder
git add Program.cs           # stage one file
git add .                    # stage everything under this folder (new, changed and deleted)
git commit -m "Add greeting" # snapshot the index, with a message
`git init` makes an empty repository: a hidden `.git` folder holding all history. Delete `.git` and the history is gone, but your files stay.
The first time on a machine, tell Git who you are, because every commit records it:

steps.prompt: Arrange the commands to create a repo and make its first commit of `Program.cs`.
steps.explain: Initialise, stage, check what will be committed, commit, then confirm it is in the history. `git status -s` before committing is a habit worth building: it shows exactly what goes in.

steps.title: What a commit is
body: A commit records a snapshot plus metadata, and is named by a **hash** of all of it:
commit 3f2a9c1e...         <- 40 hex characters; usually shortened to 7
Each commit points to its **parent**, so history is a chain read backwards from the newest:
`git log` walks that chain from newest to oldest. `git log --oneline` prints one line each: short hash and the message's first line.

steps.prompt: In a new repo you run these commands. What does `git log --oneline` print? Write the short hashes as `<h1>`, `<h2>`, ... in the order the commits were made.
code: git commit -m "Read name from args"       # makes <h2>
steps.explain: `git log` starts at the newest commit and follows parent pointers backwards, so the first commit is printed last.

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: stage changes hunk by hunk interactively, commit with a message, then show every branch's history as a graph, one line per commit.
steps.explain: `git add -p` walks through each changed hunk and asks *stage this?*, the main tool for clean, focused commits. `--all` makes `log` include every branch, not just the current one.

options: Stages changes to files Git **already tracks**, then commits. New untracked files are not included
Stages every file in the folder, including new ones, then commits
steps.explain: `-a` is a shortcut for *add modified and deleted tracked files*. A brand-new file must still be `git add`ed once. This catches people out when a new class silently misses the commit.

steps.prompt: Starting from a clean repo whose last commit contains `a.cs` and `b.cs`, what does `git status -s` print after these commands?
steps.explain: `-a` staged the change to `a.cs` and the deletion of `b.cs`, so both are in the commit and nothing is left to report for them. `c.cs` was never tracked, so `-a` ignored it.

steps.title: Your first repository
prompt: `~/notes` holds two files, `README.md` and `todo.md`, but it is not a Git repository yet.
1. Make it a repository (the default branch here is `main`).
3. Then commit `todo.md` with the message `Add todo list`.
4. Look at the result with `git log --oneline`. The working tree should be clean.

checks.name: ~/notes is a repository on main
checks.cmd: cd ~/notes && test "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" = "$HOME/notes" && test "$(git branch --show-current)" = main
checks.fail: `~/notes` is not a repository yet. `git init` inside it creates one.

checks.name: two commits, in the right order
checks.fail: `git log --reverse --format=%s` should print `Add README`, then `Add todo list`.

checks.name: the first commit has README.md only
checks.fail: The first commit should contain only `README.md`. Stage one file with `git add README.md`, not `git add .`.

checks.name: the working tree is clean
checks.fail: Something is left uncommitted. `git status` shows what.

hints: `git add README.md` stages one file; `git commit -m "Add README"` records it.
Then `git add todo.md`, `git commit -m "Add todo list"`, and `git log --oneline`.
steps.explain: `git log --oneline` shows the newest commit first, each with its short hash. The hashes differ for every learner, because a commit id covers the author and the time too.
